article.title: Cohort Analysis: Stop Mixing Customers Who Started at Different Times

paragraphs.en: A business can misread retention or spending trends when it mixes customers who joined at different times. New customers and mature customers are at different stages of their relationship, so comparing them in one aggregate can confuse customer age with calendar time. Cohort analysis solves part of this problem by grouping customers according to a shared starting event, such as acquisition month, first purchase, or subscription date. Analysts then measure behavior by time since that event. For example, instead of asking what percentage of all customers were active in September, they can ask what percentage of the January acquisition cohort remained active eight months later. This makes retention curves comparable across cohorts. The distinction is especially important during rapid growth. If many new customers enter the population, the overall average tenure falls. Aggregate spending per customer might decline even if every cohort behaves exactly as before, simply because newer customers have had less time to purchase. Conversely, a shrinking business can look artificially strong if mostly loyal long-tenure customers remain. Cohort tables can reveal whether newer groups retain better or worse than older groups at the same customer age. They can also separate lifecycle effects from calendar effects such as seasonality, inflation, or a policy change affecting everyone at once. Analysts need a precise cohort definition and a consistent denominator. Customers who churn should not silently disappear from a retention cohort. Observation windows also create censoring: recent cohorts have not yet had time to reach later months, so blank cells should not be treated as zero. Cohort analysis is not limited to retention. It can examine cumulative revenue, repeat purchase, product adoption, claims, or support usage. The method becomes most useful when the starting event has business meaning and follow-up periods are aligned consistently. Aggregate metrics answer what the population looks like today. Cohorts help explain how comparable groups evolve after a common beginning. Analysts should define the population, time window, operational constraint, and decision objective before interpreting the metric.
